exhibits.title: The Reel That Plays Any Length
exhibits.text:
An enchanted reel wound upon an hourglass frame. Ask it for a short scene and it plays crisp and true; ask it to run on and on, and something curious happens — the picture does not stop, but the longer it runs past a certain span, the more it dims, wanders, and forgets itself. The colours drift, a face slowly ceases to be the same face. It never learned to refuse a length; it simply loses conviction the further it runs beyond the horizon it was trained upon.

Here is the secret of that reel, and it is the answer to a question every practitioner asks: WHY can a video model make clips of different lengths at all, and WHY does the picture fall apart if you ask for too many seconds?

Recall the chamber before this one — the temporal weave, attention run along TIME. That attention is not fixed to a particular number of frames. The number of frames, T, is simply the SEQUENCE LENGTH it operates over — exactly as a text transformer reads sentences of many lengths without rewiring itself. Hand the model a longer temporal axis and temporal attention simply runs over more tokens. Nothing in the weights was hard-coded to one length. THAT is why the reel plays any length you ask.

But the reel was WOUND — trained — only on clips up to a certain span (for Wan, about five seconds, some eighty-one frames). Within that span it has seen how frames should hang together and it holds them steady. Run it past that span and it is improvising in country it never crossed: the picture drifts. The two plinths beside me tell how the length is free, and where the horizon lies; the lectern beyond tells why the fall is a slow slide and not a sudden cliff.

exhibits.title: T Is a Sequence Length, Not a Fixed Number
exhibits.text:
The frame count T is not carved into the weights. It is a SEQUENCE LENGTH — the number of tokens temporal attention runs over along the time axis. This is the same freedom a text transformer enjoys: it reads a sentence of five words or fifty with the identical weights, because attention is defined over however many tokens it is handed, not over a fixed count. Feed the video model a longer temporal axis and temporal attention simply attends over more frame-tokens; feed it a shorter one and it attends over fewer. Nothing needs rewiring. THIS is precisely why a single trained model can generate video of variable length.

What MAKES this freedom real is HOW such models are trained. Unlike a text model with one fixed context window, a video model is shown clips of VARIED lengths below its maximum — sometimes even mixed with single still images at T=1. Having practised many lengths, it generalises across length at inference. Varied-length training is the cause; variable-length generation is the effect. The freedom, though, has an edge — see the horizon on the lectern.

exhibits.title: The Trained Horizon (the LLM Context-Length Parallel)
exhibits.text:
There IS a ceiling, and your instinct about it is exactly right. Call it T_max: the longest clip the model was ever trained on (for Wan, about five seconds, roughly eighty-one frames at sixteen frames per second). It is set purely by what the model SAW.

Your analogy holds precisely: T_max is the video model's CONTEXT LENGTH. Running a video model past T_max is the same failure as running a language model past its trained context window. In both, attention is asked to maintain coherence over a sequence LONGER than any it learned on, and the learned patterns simply do not generalise that far. The parallel is not loose — it is the same mechanism, one axis being words and the other being frames.

Past the horizon, three things fail together. First, temporal attention never learned how frames should relate across a span that long. Second, the temporal positional encoding was never trained at those positions, so it cannot place them. Third, with nothing anchoring the picture back, error accumulates frame over frame. Consistency breaks down: drift, degradation, a face that slowly stops being itself. The reel keeps playing — it just stops being sure of what it plays.

exhibits.title: Why It Drifts — a Slide, Not a Cliff
exhibits.text:
One might expect a hard wall at T_max + 1, as though the picture shattered the instant it overstepped. It does not. The failure is a GRADUAL DRIFT — quality holds well within the trained span, then softens and wanders further and further out. Why gradual, and not a cliff?

Because long video is rarely made in one breath. It is generated in overlapping CHUNKS, each new stretch conditioned on the tail of the one before — an autoregressive handover, segment after segment. Error therefore compounds SMOOTHLY: each chunk inherits the small imperfections of its predecessor and adds its own, so the picture leans a little further from truth with every segment rather than snapping at a single frame. Compounding is a slope, not a step.

The temporal positional encoding deepens the slide. It was fitted only within the trained span; asked for positions beyond, it does not extrapolate cleanly, and its guidance degrades by degrees rather than vanishing at once. So the reel dims gradually: further past the horizon, more accumulated error, weaker positional footing, softer picture. How the chunks are actually stitched — and how Wan pushes the reel longer on purpose — waits at the Stitcher's Table beyond.

exhibits.caption: T is a sequence length, so temporal attention runs over however many frames it is given — the source of variable-length generation. Within the trained ceiling T_max, quality holds steady. Beyond it, attention never learned patterns that long and the temporal positional encoding was never trained at those positions, so the picture drifts. This is the exact failure of running a language model past its context length. Degradation is a gradual slide, not a hard cliff, because generation is chunked and error compounds smoothly.

exhibits.title: The Horizon, Charted
exhibits.caption: Study the reel's behaviour as a curve. Left: temporal coherence against generated length, measured in multiples of the trained horizon T_max (for Wan, about eighty-one frames, roughly five seconds). Within the span the model was wound upon, quality holds flat and true; past T_max it does not shatter but DRIFTS — a smooth downward slide, because long video is stitched in overlapping chunks and error compounds by degrees rather than snapping at one frame. Laid over it, in gold, is the very same-shaped fall for a language model run past its context length: not a loose analogy but one mechanism, attention asked to hold coherence over a sequence longer than any it learned on — words on one axis, frames on the other. Right: WHY the length is free at all. The training clips are of VARIED length — a heavy share of single still images at T=1, then coverage of every length up to T_max. Having practised many lengths, the model generalises across length at inference. Varied-length training is the cause; variable-length generation is the effect. Both curves are representative in shape, drawn to show the parallel, not measured benchmarks.
